paragraphs.en:
CHAPTER I
Down the Rabbit-Hole
paragraphs.zh: 第一章 · 掉进兔子洞
paragraphs.chapterTitleZh: 第一章 · 掉进兔子洞

paragraphs.en: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, `and what is the use of a book,' thought Alice `without pictures or conversation?'
paragraphs.zh: 爱丽丝和姐姐坐在河岸边，开始觉得有些无聊透顶，实在无事可做。她有一搭没一搭地瞅了一眼姐姐手里正在读的那本书，可书里既没有插图，也没有对话。“要是没有插图，也没有对话，”爱丽丝心想，“那这种书拿来又有什么用呢？”

paragraphs.en: So she was considering in her own mind (as well as she could, for the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid), whether the pleasure of making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her.
paragraphs.zh: 于是她心里开始盘算（在能力范围内尽力琢磨，毕竟炎热的天气让她感到昏昏欲睡、脑子发钝），摘野雏菊编个花环带来的乐趣，究竟值不值得她特地爬起来去采摘花朵。就在这时，一只粉红眼睛的白兔突然从她身旁飞奔而过。

paragraphs.en: There was nothing so VERY remarkable in that; nor did Alice think it so VERY much out of the way to hear the Rabbit say to itself, `Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!' (when she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural); but when the Rabbit actually TOOK A WATCH OUT OF ITS WAISTCOAT- POCKET, and looked at it, and then hurried on, Alice started to her feet, for it flashed across her mind that she had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it, and fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge.
paragraphs.zh: 这本身倒也没什么大惊小怪的，甚至当听到兔子自言自语说：“天哪！天哪！我要迟到了！”时，爱丽丝也没觉得有多么不可思议（事后想来，她才发觉自己当时理应感到惊奇，可当时一切都显得那么自然而然）。然而，当兔子竟然从背心口袋里掏出一块怀表，看了一眼便匆匆继续赶路时，爱丽丝猛地跳了起来。因为她脑海中猛然划过一个念头：她从来没见过哪只兔子居然穿有背心口袋，更没见过哪只兔子能从里面掏出一块怀表！

paragraphs.en: In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.
paragraphs.zh: 出于强烈的好奇心，她拔腿就跟着兔子穿过田野飞奔，刚好及时瞧见兔子一下子钻进了一道大树篱下方宽敞的兔子洞里。紧接着，爱丽丝也想都没想就跟着跳了进去，完全没考虑过自己究竟该怎么再爬出来。

paragraphs.en: The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.
paragraphs.zh: 兔子洞一开始像地道一样笔直向前延伸了一小段，接着突然垂直向下倾斜——甚至猝不及防到爱丽丝连片刻停步思索的机会都没有，整个人就已经身不由己地朝着一口极深的大井坠落了下去。

paragraphs.en: Either the well was very deep, or she fell very slowly, for she had plenty of time as she went down to look about her and to wonder what was going to happen next. First, she tried to look down and make out what she was coming to, but it was too dark to see anything; then she looked at the sides of the well, and noticed that they were filled with cupboards and book-shelves; here and there she saw maps and pictures hung upon pegs. She took down a jar from one of the shelves as she passed; it was labelled `ORANGE MARMALADE', but to her great disappointment it was empty: she did not like to drop the jar for fear of killing somebody, so managed to put it into one of the cupboards as she fell past it.
paragraphs.zh: 要么是这口深井实在太深，要么就是她下坠的速度极其缓慢，因为在坠落的过程中，她有充裕的时间环顾四周，琢磨接下来究竟会发生些什么。起初，她试图低头看清底下有什么，但下方一片漆黑，什么也看不见。于是她转而打量井壁，发现四周全是橱柜和书架，各处还用钉子挂着地图和图画。下落时，她顺手从架子上拿下一只罐子，上面贴着“橘子酱”的标签，可惜里面空空如也。她不敢将空罐子随手扔下去，生怕砸死底下的什么人，便在下落途中费劲地把它放进了沿途经过的另一处橱柜里。

paragraphs.en: `Well!' thought Alice to herself, `after such a fall as this, I shall think nothing of tumbling down stairs! How brave they'll all think me at home! Why, I wouldn't say anything about it, even if I fell off the top of the house!' (Which was very likely true.)
paragraphs.zh: “好家伙！”爱丽丝暗自琢磨，“经历了这么一遭摔落，以后从楼梯上滚下来我都不会当回事了！家里人肯定都会觉得我勇敢极了！哎，就算从屋顶上掉下来，我大概连吭都不会吭一声！”（这话倒是极有可能是真的。）

paragraphs.en: Down, down, down. Would the fall NEVER come to an end! `I wonder how many miles I've fallen by this time?' she said aloud. `I must be getting somewhere near the centre of the earth. Let me see: that would be four thousand miles down, I think--' (for, you see, Alice had learnt several things of this sort in her lessons in the schoolroom, and though this was not a VERY good opportunity for showing off her knowledge, as there was no one to listen to her, still it was good practice to say it over) `--yes, that's about the right distance--but then I wonder what Latitude or Longitude I've got to?' (Alice had no idea what Latitude was, or Longitude either, but thought they were nice grand words to say.)
paragraphs.zh: 下坠，下坠，无休止地下坠。难道这摔落真就没完没了吗？“真不知道我已经摔了多少英里了？”她大声自语道，“我肯定是快要接近地心附近了。让我想想：那应该有四千英里深了吧——”（因为爱丽丝在课堂上学过几门诸如此类的常识，眼下虽说绝不是炫耀知识的好时机，毕竟周围一个听众都没有，但温习一遍也挺不错的）“——对，距离差不多正是这样。可是，那我究竟到了哪一个纬度和经度呢？”（爱丽丝其实压根不知道纬度和经度到底是什么意思，但她觉得把这些气派的字眼念出来显得很有学问。）

paragraphs.en: Presently she began again. `I wonder if I shall fall right THROUGH the earth! How funny it'll seem to come out among the people that walk with their heads downward! The Antipathies, I think--' (she was rather glad there WAS no one listening, this time, as it didn't sound at all the right word) `--but I shall have to ask them what the name of the country is, you know. Please, Ma'am, is this New Zealand or Australia?' (and she tried to curtsey as she spoke--fancy CURTSEYING as you're falling through the air! Do you think you could manage it?) `And what an ignorant little girl she'll think me for asking! No, it'll never do to ask: perhaps I shall see it written up somewhere.'
paragraphs.zh: 过了一会儿，她又自言自语起来：“我会不会直接穿透地球掉出去呢？要真是从那些头朝下倒着走路的人中间钻出来，那该多滑稽啊！他们管这个叫‘对趾人’吧——”（这一回她暗自庆幸没人在听，因为这个词听起来好像完全不对）“——不过我肯定得问问他们那儿到底是什么国家。‘请问，夫人，这里是新西兰还是澳大利亚？’”（她一边说一边试着在空中屈膝行礼——试想一下，在空中凌空下坠时屈膝行礼该是多么滑稽！你觉得自己能做得到吗？）“可她要是真被我这么问，肯定会觉得我是个极其无知的小丫头！不行，绝不能开口问，也许到时候我能在哪块路牌上看到地名吧。”

paragraphs.en: Down, down, down. There was nothing else to do, so Alice soon began talking again. `Dinah'll miss me very much to-night, I should think!' (Dinah was the cat.) `I hope they'll remember her saucer of milk at tea-time. Dinah my dear! I wish you were down here with me! There are no mice in the air, I'm afraid, but you might catch a bat, and that's very like a mouse, you know. But do cats eat bats, I wonder?' And here Alice began to get rather sleepy, and went on saying to herself, in a dreamy sort of way, `Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?' and sometimes, `Do bats eat cats?' for, you see, as she couldn't answer either question, it didn't much matter which way she put it. She felt that she was dozing off, and had just begun to dream that she was walking hand in hand with Dinah, and saying to her very earnestly, `Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?' when suddenly, thump! thump! down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over.
paragraphs.zh: 下坠，下坠，继续下坠。周围实在百无聊赖，爱丽丝很快又自言自语起来。“狄娜今晚要是没我在，肯定会想死我的！”（狄娜是她家养的小猫咪。）“希望他们在下午茶时间别忘了给她盛一小碟牛奶。狄娜，我的乖乖！要是你现在能跟我一起悬在这儿该多好！不过我猜空中可没有老鼠让你逮，但你也许能抓到一只蝙蝠，你知道蝙蝠长得跟老鼠可像啦。不过，猫到底吃不吃蝙蝠呢？”说到这儿，爱丽丝开始困意袭来，嘴里含糊不清地念叨着：“猫吃蝙蝠吗？猫吃蝙蝠吗？”有时又念成：“蝙蝠吃猫吗？”因为反正是哪个问题她都回答不上来，所以颠倒过来念其实也没什么差别。她渐渐迷糊了，梦见自己正拉着狄娜的手在散步，一本正经地问它：“狄娜，快跟我说实话：你到底吃过蝙蝠没有？”就在这时——咚！噗通！她重重地跌落在一大堆枯枝败叶上，漫长的大坠落终于宣告结束！

paragraphs.en: Alice was not a bit hurt, and she jumped up on to her feet in a moment: she looked up, but it was all dark overhead; before her was another long passage, and the White Rabbit was still in sight, hurrying down it. There was not a moment to be lost: away went Alice like the wind, and was just in time to hear it say, as it turned a corner, `Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it's getting!' She was close behind it when she turned the corner, but the Rabbit was no longer to be seen: she found herself in a long, low hall, which was lit up by a row of lamps hanging from the roof.
paragraphs.zh: 爱丽丝一点儿也没摔伤，眨眼工夫便一骨碌跳了起来。她抬头张望，头顶上方一片漆黑；面前则是另一条狭长的通道，那只白兔依然在视线前方急匆匆地飞奔。片刻不可耽搁：爱丽丝宛如离弦之箭般拔腿追了上去，恰好听见它拐弯时嘴里嘀咕道：“我的耳朵和胡须啊，现在可真是太晚了！”当她跟着拐过弯时，兔子却已无影无踪，她发现自己身处一间既长又低矮的大厅里，天花板上悬挂着一排点燃的灯盏，将整座大厅照耀得通明。

paragraphs.en: There were doors all round the hall, but they were all locked; and when Alice had been all the way down one side and up the other, trying every door, she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she was ever to get out again.
paragraphs.zh: 大厅四周全是房门，但每一扇门都紧紧锁着。爱丽丝沿着一侧挨个试着推了一遍，又从另一侧走回来试了一遍，发现真的全锁住了。她不由得忧心忡忡地漫步回到大厅中央，琢磨着自己到底该怎么才能从这里走出去。

paragraphs.en: Suddenly she came upon a little three-legged table, all made of solid glass; there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice's first thought was that it might belong to one of the doors of the hall; but, alas! either the locks were too large, or the key was too small, but at any rate it would not open any of them. However, on the second time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before, and behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high: she tried the little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted!
paragraphs.zh: 忽然，她遇到了一张全用纯实心玻璃制成的三脚小桌。桌上除了放着一把极其袖珍的金钥匙外别无他物。爱丽丝首先想到的，便是这钥匙说不定能打开大厅里的某扇门。然而，天哪！要么是门锁太大，要么就是金钥匙实在太娇小，反正是哪一扇门都插不进去。不过，当她在四周绕到第二圈时，忽然注意到先前没发现的一道低矮挂帘，帘子后面赫然藏着一扇仅有大约十五英寸高的小门。她把那把小金钥匙插进锁孔，令人欣喜的是，竟然严丝合缝！

paragraphs.en: Alice opened the door and found that it led into a small passage, not much larger than a rat-hole: she knelt down and looked along the passage into the loveliest garden you ever saw. How she longed to get out of that dark hall, and wander about among those beds of bright flowers and those cool fountains, but she could not even get her head through the doorway; `and even if my head would go through,' thought poor Alice, `it would be of very little use without my shoulders. Oh, how I wish I could shut up like a telescope! I think I could, if I only know how to begin.' For, you see, so many out-of-the-way things had happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things indeed were really impossible.
paragraphs.zh: 爱丽丝推开小门，发现门后连着一条狭窄的通道，大小不过堪比一个老鼠洞。她跪下身朝通道深处望去，眼前展现出一处她所见过的最美丽的花园。她多么渴望能离开这间阴暗的大厅，漫步在那些绚烂的花坛和清凉的喷泉之间！然而，她甚至连脑袋都塞不进门洞。“就算我的脑袋能钻过去，”可怜的爱丽丝心想，“没有肩膀跟着过去又有什么用呢。啊，要是我能像望远镜一样折叠收缩起来该多好啊！我想我肯定能做到的，只要我掌握了折叠的诀窍就行。”毕竟，最近接二连三发生的不可思议的奇事，已经让爱丽丝觉得天下几乎没有什么事情是真正不可能发生的了。

paragraphs.en: There seemed to be no use in waiting by the little door, so she went back to the table, half hoping she might find another key on it, or at any rate a book of rules for shutting people up like telescopes: this time she found a little bottle on it, (`which certainly was not here before,' said Alice,) and round the neck of the bottle was a paper label, with the words `DRINK ME' beautifully printed on it in large letters.
paragraphs.zh: 在小门边守候似乎毫无意义，于是她折返回到玻璃桌旁，隐隐期盼能在上面再找到另一把钥匙，或者至少是一本教人如何把身体像望远镜一样折叠收缩的指南秘籍。这一次，她在桌上赫然发现了一只小巧的玻璃瓶（“刚才那儿绝对是没有这瓶子的，”爱丽丝说）。小瓶的瓶颈上系着一张精致的纸标签，上面用优美的大号印刷体醒目地印着：“喝我”。

paragraphs.en: It was all very well to say `Drink me,' but the wise little Alice was not going to do THAT in a hurry. `No, I'll look first,' she said, `and see whether it's marked "poison" or not'; for she had read several nice little histories about children who had got burnt, and eaten up by wild beasts and other unpleasant things, all because they WOULD not remember the simple rules their friends had taught them: such as, that a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long; and that if you cut your finger VERY deeply with a knife, it usually bleeds; and she had never forgotten that, if you drink much from a bottle marked `poison,' it is almost certain to disagree with you, sooner or later.
paragraphs.zh: 瓶上写着“喝我”固然亲切，但聪慧的小爱丽丝可不会盲目照做。“不行，我得先仔细瞧瞧，”她说，“看看上面到底有没有标明‘有毒’二字。”因为她听过不少关于小孩子的真实悲惨故事：有的孩子就因为不听劝告，被烈火烧伤，或是从悬崖摔下；这全是因为他们记不住大人的谆谆教诲——比如，要是你把烧红的火钳握得太久，肯定会被烫伤；要是你用小刀在手指上割得太深，通常都会流血；而最重要的一条法则她永远铭记在心：如果你把标有‘有毒’字样的药水喝下一大堆，十有八九迟早会让你痛不欲生。

paragraphs.en: However, this bottle was NOT marked `poison,' so Alice ventured to taste it, and finding it very nice, (it had, in fact, a sort of mixed flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast,) she very soon finished it off.
paragraphs.zh: 不过，这只瓶子上确实没有标明“有毒”。于是爱丽丝大着胆子尝了一小口，发觉滋味好极了（味道简直就像樱桃馅饼、奶油蛋羹、菠萝、烤火鸡、太妃糖和热黄油吐司的混合风味），没过多久，她就干脆一口气把整瓶药水喝了个精光。

paragraphs.en: `What a curious feeling!' said Alice; `I must be shutting up like a telescope.'
paragraphs.zh: “多么奇异奇妙的感觉啊！”爱丽丝惊叹道，“我一定是在像望远镜一样缩拢了！”

paragraphs.en: And so it was indeed: she was now only ten inches high, and her face brightened up at the thought that she was now the right size for going through the little door into that lovely garden. First, however, she waited for a few minutes to see if she was going to shrink any further: she felt a little nervous about this; `for it might end, you know,' said Alice to herself, `in my going out altogether, like a candle. I wonder what I should be like then?' And she tried to fancy what the flame of a candle is like after the candle is blown out, for she could not remember ever having seen such a thing.
paragraphs.zh: 事实确实如此：她此刻居然缩得只有十英寸高了！一想到自己现在的大小正适合穿过那扇通往美丽花园的小门，她的脸庞瞬间容光焕发。不过，她决定先耐着性子等待几分钟，看看自己会不会继续变小下去；她为此感到了一丝隐隐的慌张，“因为你们知道，”爱丽丝自言自语道，“这最终很有可能会让我彻底化为乌有，就像蜡烛熄灭了一样。到那时我究竟会变成什么样呢？”她绞尽脑汁试图想象蜡烛熄灭之后火焰究竟是个什么模样，因为她从来没见过这种景象。

paragraphs.en: After a while, finding that nothing more happened, she decided on going into the garden at once; but, alas for poor Alice! when she got to the door, she found she had forgotten the little golden key, and when she went back to the table for it, she found she could not possibly reach it: she could see it quite plainly through the glass, and she tried her best to climb up one of the legs of the table, but it was too slippery; and when she had tired herself out with trying, the poor little thing sat down and cried.
paragraphs.zh: 等了一会儿，发现自己并没有进一步缩小，她便兴高采烈地决定立刻动身前往那座美丽的花园。然而，呜呼哀哉！当可怜的小爱丽丝赶到门前时，才发觉自己把那把小金钥匙落在了玻璃桌上；而当她折返回到桌旁时，绝望地发现自己根本够不着了！她透过通透的玻璃能清清楚楚地看到钥匙就在上面，于是她使出浑身解数试图顺着光滑的玻璃桌腿往上攀爬，可桌腿实在太滑了。在一次次滑落折腾得精疲力竭之后，可怜的小姑娘终于一屁股坐在地上痛哭流涕起来。

paragraphs.en: `Come, there's no use in crying like that!' said Alice to herself, rather sharply; `I advise you to leave off this minute!' She generally gave herself very good advice, (though she very seldom followed it), and sometimes she scolded herself so severely as to bring tears into her eyes; and once she remembered trying to box her own ears for having cheated herself in a game of croquet she was playing against herself, for this curious child was very fond of pretending to be two people. `But it's no use now,' thought poor Alice, `to pretend to be two people! Why, there's hardly enough of me left to make ONE respectable person!'
paragraphs.zh: “快得了吧，像这样哭哭啼啼根本无济于事！”爱丽丝毫不客气地严厉斥责起自己，“我限你一分钟之内立刻收起眼泪！”她通常总是给自己提出非常明智的中肯忠告（虽然她很少真正遵照执行），有时她甚至严厉地把自己训斥得泪流满面。她还依稀记得有一回，就因为自己在单人槌球游戏里欺骗了自己，她甚至扬言要扇自己耳光。这个古怪的小姑娘非常热衷于一人分饰两角，假装自己是两个不同的人。“可是眼下假装成两个人还有什么用呢！”可怜的爱丽丝心想，“我剩下的这丁点儿身躯，就连凑成一个像模像样的人都不够看了！”

paragraphs.en: Soon her eye fell on a little glass box that was lying under the table: she opened it, and found in it a very small cake, on which the words `EAT ME' were beautifully marked in currants. `Well, I'll eat it,' said Alice, `and if it makes me grow larger, I can reach the key; and if it makes me grow smaller, I can creep under the door; so either way I'll get into the garden, and I don't care which happens!'
paragraphs.zh: 不久，她的目光落在了玻璃桌下方的一只小玻璃盒子上。她打开盒子，发现里面装着一块精美的小蛋糕，上面用葡萄干整整齐齐地拼嵌出两个字：“吃我”。“好吧，那我就把它吃掉，”爱丽丝说，“如果它能让我变大，我就能够得着桌上的金钥匙；如果它让我变得更小，我也能从小门缝底下钻过去。反正不管变成哪样我都能进到花园里去，所以我才不在乎到底会怎样呢！”

paragraphs.en: She ate a little bit, and said anxiously to herself, `Which way? Which way?', holding her hand on the top of her head to feel which way it was growing, and she was quite surprised to find that she remained the same size: to be sure, this generally happens when one eats cake, but Alice had got so much into the way of expecting nothing but out-of-the-way things to happen, that it seemed quite dull and stupid for life to go on in the common way.
paragraphs.zh: 她小心翼翼地咬了一小块，急切地将手按在头顶上自语道：“到底是哪边？往哪边长？”以便随时感知自己究竟是向上长还是向下缩。然而，令她大惑不解的是，自己的个头居然纹丝未动。当然，正常人吃蛋糕本来就不会改变身高，但爱丽丝最近早已习惯了身旁接二连三发生的不可思议的奇迹，在她看来，生活若是一切按部就班反倒显得单调乏味了。

paragraphs.en: So she set to work, and very soon finished off the cake.
paragraphs.zh: 于是她不再迟疑，索性放开胃口大嚼起来，三下五除二便将整块小蛋糕吃得一干二净。

paragraphs.en:
CHAPTER II
The Pool of Tears
paragraphs.zh: 第二章 · 眼泪的池塘
paragraphs.chapterTitleZh: 第二章 · 眼泪的池塘

paragraphs.en: `Curiouser and curiouser!' cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English); `now I'm opening out like the largest telescope that ever was! Good-bye, feet!' (for when she looked down at her feet, they seemed to be almost out of sight, they were getting so far off). `Oh, my poor little feet, I wonder who will put on your shoes and stockings for you now, dears? I'm sure _I_ shan't be able! I shall be a great deal too far off to trouble myself about you: you must manage the best way you can; --but I must be kind to them,' thought Alice, `or perhaps they won't walk the way I want to go! Let me see: I'll give them a new pair of boots every Christmas.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 1 段）

paragraphs.en: And she went on planning to herself how she would manage it. `They must go by the carrier,' she thought; `and how funny it'll seem, sending presents to one's own feet! And how odd the directions will look!
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 2 段）

paragraphs.en: ALICE'S RIGHT FOOT, ESQ. HEARTHRUG, NEAR THE FENDER, (WITH ALICE'S LOVE).
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 3 段）

paragraphs.en: Oh dear, what nonsense I'm talking!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 4 段）

paragraphs.en: Just then her head struck against the roof of the hall: in fact she was now more than nine feet high, and she at once took up the little golden key and hurried off to the garden door.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 5 段）

paragraphs.en: Poor Alice! It was as much as she could do, lying down on one side, to look through into the garden with one eye; but to get through was more hopeless than ever: she sat down and began to cry again.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 6 段）

paragraphs.en: `You ought to be ashamed of yourself,' said Alice, `a great girl like you,' (she might well say this), `to go on crying in this way! Stop this moment, I tell you!' But she went on all the same, shedding gallons of tears, until there was a large pool all round her, about four inches deep and reaching half down the hall.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 7 段）

paragraphs.en: After a time she heard a little pattering of feet in the distance, and she hastily dried her eyes to see what was coming. It was the White Rabbit returning, splendidly dressed, with a pair of white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other: he came trotting along in a great hurry, muttering to himself as he came, `Oh! the Duchess, the Duchess! Oh! won't she be savage if I've kept her waiting!' Alice felt so desperate that she was ready to ask help of any one; so, when the Rabbit came near her, she began, in a low, timid voice, `If you please, sir--' The Rabbit started violently, dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and skurried away into the darkness as hard as he could go.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 8 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice took up the fan and gloves, and, as the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself all the time she went on talking: `Dear, dear! How queer everything is to-day! And yesterday things went on just as usual. I wonder if I've been changed in the night? Let me think: was I the same when I got up this morning? I almost think I can remember feeling a little different. But if I'm not the same, the next question is, Who in the world am I? Ah, THAT'S the great puzzle!' And she began thinking over all the children she knew that were of the same age as herself, to see if she could have been changed for any of them.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 9 段）

paragraphs.en: `I'm sure I'm not Ada,' she said, `for her hair goes in such long ringlets, and mine doesn't go in ringlets at all; and I'm sure I can't be Mabel, for I know all sorts of things, and she, oh! she knows such a very little! Besides, SHE'S she, and I'm I, and--oh dear, how puzzling it all is! I'll try if I know all the things I used to know. Let me see: four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen, and four times seven is--oh dear! I shall never get to twenty at that rate! However, the Multiplication Table doesn't signify: let's try Geography. London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome, and Rome--no, THAT'S all wrong, I'm certain! I must have been changed for Mabel! I'll try and say "How doth the little--"' and she crossed her hands on her lap as if she were saying lessons, and began to repeat it, but her voice sounded hoarse and strange, and the words did not come the same as they used to do:--
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 10 段）

paragraphs.en: `How doth the little crocodile Improve his shining tail, And pour the waters of the Nile On every golden scale!
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 11 段）

paragraphs.en: `How cheerfully he seems to grin, How neatly spread his claws, And welcome little fishes in With gently smiling jaws!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 12 段）

paragraphs.en: `I'm sure those are not the right words,' said poor Alice, and her eyes filled with tears again as she went on, `I must be Mabel after all, and I shall have to go and live in that poky little house, and have next to no toys to play with, and oh! ever so many lessons to learn! No, I've made up my mind about it; if I'm Mabel, I'll stay down here! It'll be no use their putting their heads down and saying "Come up again, dear!" I shall only look up and say "Who am I then? Tell me that first, and then, if I like being that person, I'll come up: if not, I'll stay down here till I'm somebody else"--but, oh dear!' cried Alice, with a sudden burst of tears, `I do wish they WOULD put their heads down! I am so VERY tired of being all alone here!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 13 段）

paragraphs.en: As she said this she looked down at her hands, and was surprised to see that she had put on one of the Rabbit's little white kid gloves while she was talking. `How CAN I have done that?' she thought. `I must be growing small again.' She got up and went to the table to measure herself by it, and found that, as nearly as she could guess, she was now about two feet high, and was going on shrinking rapidly: she soon found out that the cause of this was the fan she was holding, and she dropped it hastily, just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 14 段）

paragraphs.en: `That WAS a narrow escape!' said Alice, a good deal frightened at the sudden change, but very glad to find herself still in existence; `and now for the garden!' and she ran with all speed back to the little door: but, alas! the little door was shut again, and the little golden key was lying on the glass table as before, `and things are worse than ever,' thought the poor child, `for I never was so small as this before, never! And I declare it's too bad, that it is!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 15 段）

paragraphs.en: As she said these words her foot slipped, and in another moment, splash! she was up to her chin in salt water. Her first idea was that she had somehow fallen into the sea, `and in that case I can go back by railway,' she said to herself. (Alice had been to the seaside once in her life, and had come to the general conclusion, that wherever you go to on the English coast you find a number of bathing machines in the sea, some children digging in the sand with wooden spades, then a row of lodging houses, and behind them a railway station.) However, she soon made out that feet high.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 16 段）

paragraphs.en: `I wish I hadn't cried so much!' said Alice, as she swam about, trying to find her way out. `I shall be punished for it now, I suppose, by being drowned in my own tears! That WILL be a queer thing, to be sure! However, everything is queer to-day.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 17 段）

paragraphs.en: Just then she heard something splashing about in the pool a little way off, and she swam nearer to make out what it was: at first she thought it must be a walrus or hippopotamus, but then she remembered how small she was now, and she soon made out that it was only a mouse that had slipped in like herself.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 18 段）

paragraphs.en: `Would it be of any use, now,' thought Alice, `to speak to this mouse? Everything is so out-of-the-way down here, that I should think very likely it can talk: at any rate, there's no harm in trying.' So she began: `O Mouse, do you know the way out of this pool? I am very tired of swimming about here, O Mouse!' (Alice thought this must be the right way of speaking to a mouse: she had never done such a thing before, but she remembered having seen in her brother's Latin Grammar, `A mouse--of a mouse--to a mouse--a mouse--O mouse!') The Mouse looked at her rather inquisitively, and seemed to her to wink with one of its little eyes, but it said nothing.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 19 段）

paragraphs.en: `Perhaps it doesn't understand English,' thought Alice; `I daresay it's a French mouse, come over with William the Conqueror.' (For, with all her knowledge of history, Alice had no very clear notion how long ago anything had happened.) So she began again: `Ou est ma chatte?' which was the first sentence in her French lesson-book. The Mouse gave a sudden leap out of the water, and seemed to quiver all over with fright. `Oh, I beg your pardon!' cried Alice hastily, afraid that she had hurt the poor animal's feelings. `I quite forgot you didn't like cats.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 20 段）

paragraphs.en: `Not like cats!' cried the Mouse, in a shrill, passionate voice. `Would YOU like cats if you were me?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 21 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, perhaps not,' said Alice in a soothing tone: `don't be angry about it. And yet I wish I could show you our cat Dinah: I think you'd take a fancy to cats if you could only see her. She is such a dear quiet thing,' Alice went on, half to herself, as she swam lazily about in the pool, `and she sits purring so nicely by the fire, licking her paws and washing her face--and she is such a nice soft thing to nurse--and she's such a capital one for catching mice--oh, I beg your pardon!' cried Alice again, for this time the Mouse was bristling all over, and she felt certain it must be really offended. `We won't talk about her any more if you'd rather not.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 22 段）

paragraphs.en: `We indeed!' cried the Mouse, who was trembling down to the end of his tail. `As if I would talk on such a subject! Our family always HATED cats: nasty, low, vulgar things! Don't let me hear the name again!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 23 段）

paragraphs.en: `I won't indeed!' said Alice, in a great hurry to change the subject of conversation. `Are you--are you fond--of--of dogs?' The Mouse did not answer, so Alice went on eagerly: `There is such a nice little dog near our house I should like to show you! A little bright-eyed terrier, you know, with oh, such long curly brown hair! And it'll fetch things when you throw them, and it'll sit up and beg for its dinner, and all sorts of things--I can't remember half of them--and it belongs to a farmer, you know, and he says it's so useful, it's worth a hundred pounds! He says it kills all the rats and--oh dear!' cried Alice in a sorrowful tone, `I'm afraid I've offended it again!' For the Mouse was swimming away from her as hard as it could go, and making quite a commotion in the pool as it went.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 24 段）

paragraphs.en: So she called softly after it, `Mouse dear! Do come back again, and we won't talk about cats or dogs either, if you don't like them!' When the Mouse heard this, it turned round and swam slowly back to her: its face was quite pale (with passion, Alice thought), and it said in a low trembling voice, `Let us get to the shore, and then I'll tell you my history, and you'll understand why it is I hate cats and dogs.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 25 段）

paragraphs.en: It was high time to go, for the pool was getting quite crowded with the birds and animals that had fallen into it: there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet, and several other curious creatures. Alice led the way, and the whole party swam to the shore.
paragraphs.zh: （第 2 章 · 眼泪的池塘 第 26 段）

paragraphs.en:
CHAPTER III
A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
paragraphs.zh: 第三章 · 政治集会赛跑与长长的故事
paragraphs.chapterTitleEn: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
paragraphs.chapterTitleZh: 第三章 · 政治集会赛跑与长长的故事

paragraphs.en: They were indeed a queer-looking party that assembled on the bank--the birds with draggled feathers, the animals with their fur clinging close to them, and all dripping wet, cross, and uncomfortable.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 1 段）

paragraphs.en: The first question of course was, how to get dry again: they had a consultation about this, and after a few minutes it seemed quite natural to Alice to find herself talking familiarly with them, as if she had known them all her life. Indeed, she had quite a long argument with the Lory, who at last turned sulky, and would only say, `I am older than you, and must know better'; and this Alice would not allow without knowing how old it was, and, as the Lory positively refused to tell its age, there was no more to be said.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 2 段）

paragraphs.en: At last the Mouse, who seemed to be a person of authority among them, called out, `Sit down, all of you, and listen to me! I'LL soon make you dry enough!' They all sat down at once, in a large ring, with the Mouse in the middle. Alice kept her eyes anxiously fixed on it, for she felt sure she would catch a bad cold if she did not get dry very soon.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 3 段）

paragraphs.en: `Ahem!' said the Mouse with an important air, `are you all ready? This is the driest thing I know. Silence all round, if you please! "William the Conqueror, whose cause was favoured by the pope, was soon submitted to by the English, who wanted leaders, and had been of late much accustomed to usurpation and conquest. Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria--"'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 4 段）

paragraphs.en: `Ugh!' said the Lory, with a shiver.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 5 段）

paragraphs.en: `I beg your pardon!' said the Mouse, frowning, but very politely: `Did you speak?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 6 段）

paragraphs.en: `Not I!' said the Lory hastily.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 7 段）

paragraphs.en: `I thought you did,' said the Mouse. `--I proceed. "Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria, declared for him: and even Stigand, the patriotic archbishop of Canterbury, found it advisable--"'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 8 段）

paragraphs.en: `Found WHAT?' said the Duck.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 9 段）

paragraphs.en: `Found IT,' the Mouse replied rather crossly: `of course you know what "it" means.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 10 段）

paragraphs.en: `I know what "it" means well enough, when I find a thing,' said the Duck: `it's generally a frog or a worm. The question is, what did the archbishop find?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 11 段）

paragraphs.en: The Mouse did not notice this question, but hurriedly went on, `"--found it advisable to go with Edgar Atheling to meet William and offer him the crown. William's conduct at first was moderate. But the insolence of his Normans--" How are you getting on now, my dear?' it continued, turning to Alice as it spoke.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 12 段）

paragraphs.en: `As wet as ever,' said Alice in a melancholy tone: `it doesn't seem to dry me at all.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 13 段）

paragraphs.en: `In that case,' said the Dodo solemnly, rising to its feet, `I move that the meeting adjourn, for the immediate adoption of more energetic remedies--'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 14 段）

paragraphs.en: `Speak English!' said the Eaglet. `I don't know the meaning of half those long words, and, what's more, I don't believe you do either!' And the Eaglet bent down its head to hide a smile: some of the other birds tittered audibly.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 15 段）

paragraphs.en: `What I was going to say,' said the Dodo in an offended tone, `was, that the best thing to get us dry would be a Caucus-race.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 16 段）

paragraphs.en: `What IS a Caucus-race?' said Alice; not that she wanted much to know, but the Dodo had paused as if it thought that SOMEBODY ought to speak, and no one else seemed inclined to say anything.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 17 段）

paragraphs.en: `Why,' said the Dodo, `the best way to explain it is to do it.' (And, as you might like to try the thing yourself, some winter day, I will tell you how the Dodo managed it.)
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 18 段）

paragraphs.en: First it marked out a race-course, in a sort of circle, (`the exact shape doesn't matter,' it said,) and then all the party were placed along the course, here and there. There was no `One, two, three, and away,' but they began running when they liked, and left off when they liked, so that it was not easy to know when the race was over. However, when they had been running half an hour or so, and were quite dry again, the Dodo suddenly called out `The race is over!' and they all crowded round it, panting, and asking, `But who has won?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 19 段）

paragraphs.en: This question the Dodo could not answer without a great deal of thought, and it sat for a long time with one finger pressed upon its forehead (the position in which you usually see Shakespeare, in the pictures of him), while the rest waited in silence. At last the Dodo said, `EVERYBODY has won, and all must have prizes.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 20 段）

paragraphs.en: `But who is to give the prizes?' quite a chorus of voices asked.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 21 段）

paragraphs.en: `Why, SHE, of course,' said the Dodo, pointing to Alice with one finger; and the whole party at once crowded round her, calling out in a confused way, `Prizes! Prizes!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 22 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice had no idea what to do, and in despair she put her hand in her pocket, and pulled out a box of comfits, (luckily the salt water had not got into it), and handed them round as prizes. There was exactly one a-piece all round.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 23 段）

paragraphs.en: `But she must have a prize herself, you know,' said the Mouse.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 24 段）

paragraphs.en: `Of course,' the Dodo replied very gravely. `What else have you got in your pocket?' he went on, turning to Alice.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 25 段）

paragraphs.en: `Only a thimble,' said Alice sadly.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 26 段）

paragraphs.en: `Hand it over here,' said the Dodo.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 27 段）

paragraphs.en: Then they all crowded round her once more, while the Dodo solemnly presented the thimble, saying `We beg your acceptance of this elegant thimble'; and, when it had finished this short speech, they all cheered.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 28 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice thought the whole thing very absurd, but they all looked so grave that she did not dare to laugh; and, as she could not think of anything to say, she simply bowed, and took the thimble, looking as solemn as she could.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 29 段）

paragraphs.en: The next thing was to eat the comfits: this caused some noise and confusion, as the large birds complained that they could not taste theirs, and the small ones choked and had to be patted on the back. However, it was over at last, and they sat down again in a ring, and begged the Mouse to tell them something more.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 30 段）

paragraphs.en: `You promised to tell me your history, you know,' said Alice, `and why it is you hate--C and D,' she added in a whisper, half afraid that it would be offended again.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 31 段）

paragraphs.en: `Mine is a long and a sad tale!' said the Mouse, turning to Alice, and sighing.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 32 段）

paragraphs.en: `It IS a long tail, certainly,' said Alice, looking down with wonder at the Mouse's tail; `but why do you call it sad?' And she kept on puzzling about it while the Mouse was speaking, so that her idea of the tale was something like this:--
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 33 段）

paragraphs.en: `Fury said to a mouse, That he met in the house, "Let us both go to law: I will prosecute YOU. --Come, I'll take no denial; We must have a trial: For really this morning I've nothing to do." Said the mouse to the cur, "Such a trial, dear Sir, With no jury or judge, would be wasting our breath." "I'll be judge, I'll be jury," Said cunning old Fury: "I'll try the whole cause, and condemn you to death."'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 34 段）

paragraphs.en: `You are not attending!' said the Mouse to Alice severely. `What are you thinking of?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 35 段）

paragraphs.en: `I beg your pardon,' said Alice very humbly: `you had got to the fifth bend, I think?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 36 段）

paragraphs.en: `I had NOT!' cried the Mouse, sharply and very angrily.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 37 段）

paragraphs.en: `A knot!' said Alice, always ready to make herself useful, and looking anxiously about her. `Oh, do let me help to undo it!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 38 段）

paragraphs.en: `I shall do nothing of the sort,' said the Mouse, getting up and walking away. `You insult me by talking such nonsense!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 39 段）

paragraphs.en: `I didn't mean it!' pleaded poor Alice. `But you're so easily offended, you know!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 40 段）

paragraphs.en: The Mouse only growled in reply.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 41 段）

paragraphs.en: `Please come back and finish your story!' Alice called after it; and the others all joined in chorus, `Yes, please do!' but the Mouse only shook its head impatiently, and walked a little quicker.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 42 段）

paragraphs.en: `What a pity it wouldn't stay!' sighed the Lory, as soon as it was quite out of sight; and an old Crab took the opportunity of saying to her daughter `Ah, my dear! Let this be a lesson to you never to lose YOUR temper!' `Hold your tongue, Ma!' said the young Crab, a little snappishly. `You're enough to try the patience of an oyster!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 43 段）

paragraphs.en: `I wish I had our Dinah here, I know I do!' said Alice aloud, addressing nobody in particular. `She'd soon fetch it back!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 44 段）

paragraphs.en: `And who is Dinah, if I might venture to ask the question?' said the Lory.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 45 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice replied eagerly, for she was always ready to talk about her pet: `Dinah's our cat. And she's such a capital one for catching mice you can't think! And oh, I wish you could see her after the birds! Why, she'll eat a little bird as soon as look at it!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 46 段）

paragraphs.en: This speech caused a remarkable sensation among the party. Some of the birds hurried off at once: one old Magpie began wrapping itself up very carefully, remarking, `I really must be getting home; the night-air doesn't suit my throat!' and a Canary called out in a trembling voice to its children, `Come away, my dears! It's high time you were all in bed!' On various pretexts they all moved off, and Alice was soon left alone.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 47 段）

paragraphs.en: `I wish I hadn't mentioned Dinah!' she said to herself in a melancholy tone. `Nobody seems to like her, down here, and I'm sure she's the best cat in the world! Oh, my dear Dinah! I wonder if I shall ever see you any more!' And here poor Alice began to cry again, for she felt very lonely and low-spirited. In a little while, however, she again heard a little pattering of footsteps in the distance, and she looked up eagerly, half hoping that the Mouse had changed his mind, and was coming back to finish his story.
paragraphs.zh: （第 3 章 · 热身赛跑与长长的故事 第 48 段）

paragraphs.en:
CHAPTER IV
The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
paragraphs.zh: 第四章 · 白兔差遣小比尔
paragraphs.chapterTitleEn: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
paragraphs.chapterTitleZh: 第四章 · 白兔差遣小比尔

paragraphs.en: It was the White Rabbit, trotting slowly back again, and looking anxiously about as it went, as if it had lost something; and she heard it muttering to itself `The Duchess! The Duchess! Oh my dear paws! Oh my fur and whiskers! She'll get me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets! Where CAN I have dropped them, I wonder?' Alice guessed in a moment that it was looking for the fan and the pair of white kid gloves, and she very good-naturedly began hunting about for them, but they were nowhere to be seen--everything seemed to have changed since her swim in the pool, and the great hall, with the glass table and the little door, had vanished completely.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 1 段）

paragraphs.en: Very soon the Rabbit noticed Alice, as she went hunting about, and called out to her in an angry tone, `Why, Mary Ann, what ARE you doing out here? Run home this moment, and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan! Quick, now!' And Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed to, without trying to explain the mistake it had made.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 2 段）

paragraphs.en: `He took me for his housemaid,' she said to herself as she ran. `How surprised he'll be when he finds out who I am! But I'd better take him his fan and gloves--that is, if I can find them.' As she said this, she came upon a neat little house, on the door of which was a bright brass plate with the name `W. RABBIT' engraved upon it. She went in without knocking, and hurried upstairs, in great fear lest she should meet the real Mary Ann, and be turned out of the house before she had found the fan and gloves.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 3 段）

paragraphs.en: `How queer it seems,' Alice said to herself, `to be going messages for a rabbit! I suppose Dinah'll be sending me on messages next!' And she began fancying the sort of thing that would happen: `"Miss Alice! Come here directly, and get ready for your walk!" "Coming in a minute, nurse! But I've got to see that the mouse doesn't get out." Only I don't think,' Alice went on, `that they'd let Dinah stop in the house if it began ordering people about like that!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 4 段）

paragraphs.en: By this time she had found her way into a tidy little room with a table in the window, and on it (as she had hoped) a fan and two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves: she took up the fan and a pair of the gloves, and was just going to leave the room, when her eye fell upon a little bottle that stood near the looking- glass. There was no label this time with the words `DRINK ME,' but nevertheless she uncorked it and put it to her lips. `I know SOMETHING interesting is sure to happen,' she said to herself, `whenever I eat or drink anything; so I'll just see what this bottle does. I do hope it'll make me grow large again, for really I'm quite tired of being such a tiny little thing!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 5 段）

paragraphs.en: It did so indeed, and much sooner than she had expected: before she had drunk half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling, and had to stoop to save her neck from being broken. She hastily put down the bottle, saying to herself `That's quite enough--I hope I shan't grow any more--As it is, I can't get out at the door--I do wish I hadn't drunk quite so much!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 6 段）

paragraphs.en: Alas! it was too late to wish that! She went on growing, and growing, and very soon had to kneel down on the floor: in another minute there was not even room for this, and she tried the effect of lying down with one elbow against the door, and the other arm curled round her head. Still she went on growing, and, as a last resource, she put one arm out of the window, and one foot up the chimney, and said to herself `Now I can do no more, whatever happens. What WILL become of me?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 7 段）

paragraphs.en: Luckily for Alice, the little magic bottle had now had its full effect, and she grew no larger: still it was very uncomfortable, and, as there seemed to be no sort of chance of her ever getting out of the room again, no wonder she felt unhappy.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 8 段）

paragraphs.en: `It was much pleasanter at home,' thought poor Alice, `when one wasn't always growing larger and smaller, and being ordered about by mice and rabbits. I almost wish I hadn't gone down that rabbit-hole--and yet--and yet--it's rather curious, you know, this sort of life! I do wonder what CAN have happened to me! When I used to read fairy-tales, I fancied that kind of thing never happened, and now here I am in the middle of one! There ought to be a book written about me, that there ought! And when I grow up, I'll write one--but I'm grown up now,' she added in a sorrowful tone; `at least there's no room to grow up any more HERE.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 9 段）

paragraphs.en: `But then,' thought Alice, `shall I NEVER get any older than I am now? That'll be a comfort, one way--never to be an old woman-- but then--always to have lessons to learn! Oh, I shouldn't like THAT!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 10 段）

paragraphs.en: `Oh, you foolish Alice!' she answered herself. `How can you learn lessons in here? Why, there's hardly room for YOU, and no room at all for any lesson-books!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 11 段）

paragraphs.en: And so she went on, taking first one side and then the other, and making quite a conversation of it altogether; but after a few minutes she heard a voice outside, and stopped to listen.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 12 段）

paragraphs.en: `Mary Ann! Mary Ann!' said the voice. `Fetch me my gloves this moment!' Then came a little pattering of feet on the stairs. Alice knew it was the Rabbit coming to look for her, and she trembled till she shook the house, quite forgetting that she was now about a thousand times as large as the Rabbit, and had no reason to be afraid of it.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 13 段）

paragraphs.en: Presently the Rabbit came up to the door, and tried to open it; but, as the door opened inwards, and Alice's elbow was pressed hard against it, that attempt proved a failure. Alice heard it say to itself `Then I'll go round and get in at the window.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 14 段）

paragraphs.en: `THAT you won't' thought Alice, and, after waiting till she fancied she heard the Rabbit just under the window, she suddenly spread out her hand, and made a snatch in the air. She did not get hold of anything, but she heard a little shriek and a fall, and a crash of broken glass, from which she concluded that it was just possible it had fallen into a cucumber-frame, or something of the sort.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 15 段）

paragraphs.en: Next came an angry voice--the Rabbit's--`Pat! Pat! Where are you?' And then a voice she had never heard before, `Sure then I'm here! Digging for apples, yer honour!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 16 段）

paragraphs.en: `Digging for apples, indeed!' said the Rabbit angrily. `Here! Come and help me out of THIS!' (Sounds of more broken glass.)
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 17 段）

paragraphs.en: `Now tell me, Pat, what's that in the window?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 18 段）

paragraphs.en: `Sure, it's an arm, yer honour!' (He pronounced it `arrum.')
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 19 段）

paragraphs.en: `An arm, you goose! Who ever saw one that size? Why, it fills the whole window!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 20 段）

paragraphs.en: `Sure, it does, yer honour: but it's an arm for all that.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 21 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, it's got no business there, at any rate: go and take it away!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 22 段）

paragraphs.en: There was a long silence after this, and Alice could only hear whispers now and then; such as, `Sure, I don't like it, yer honour, at all, at all!' `Do as I tell you, you coward!' and at last she spread out her hand again, and made another snatch in the air. This time there were TWO little shrieks, and more sounds of broken glass. `What a number of cucumber-frames there must be!' thought Alice. `I wonder what they'll do next! As for pulling me out of the window, I only wish they COULD! I'm sure I don't want to stay in here any longer!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 23 段）

paragraphs.en: She waited for some time without hearing anything more: at last came a rumbling of little cartwheels, and the sound of a good many voices all talking together: she made out the words: `Where's the other ladder?--Why, I hadn't to bring but one; Bill's got the other--Bill! fetch it here, lad!--Here, put 'em up at this corner--No, tie 'em together first--they don't reach half high enough yet--Oh! they'll do well enough; don't be particular-- Here, Bill! catch hold of this rope--Will the roof bear?--Mind that loose slate--Oh, it's coming down! Heads below!' (a loud crash)--`Now, who did that?--It was Bill, I fancy--Who's to go down the chimney?--Nay, I shan't! YOU do it!--That I won't, then!--Bill's to go down--Here, Bill! the master says you're to go down the chimney!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 24 段）

paragraphs.en: `Oh! So Bill's got to come down the chimney, has he?' said Alice to herself. `Shy, they seem to put everything upon Bill! I wouldn't be in Bill's place for a good deal: this fireplace is narrow, to be sure; but I THINK I can kick a little!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 25 段）

paragraphs.en: She drew her foot as far down the chimney as she could, and waited till she heard a little animal (she couldn't guess of what sort it was) scratching and scrambling about in the chimney close above her: then, saying to herself `This is Bill,' she gave one sharp kick, and waited to see what would happen next.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 26 段）

paragraphs.en: The first thing she heard was a general chorus of `There goes Bill!' then the Rabbit's voice along--`Catch him, you by the hedge!' then silence, and then another confusion of voices--`Hold up his head--Brandy now--Don't choke him--How was it, old fellow? What happened to you? Tell us all about it!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 27 段）

paragraphs.en: Last came a little feeble, squeaking voice, (`That's Bill,' thought Alice,) `Well, I hardly know--No more, thank ye; I'm better now--but I'm a deal too flustered to tell you--all I know is, something comes at me like a Jack-in-the-box, and up I goes like a sky-rocket!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 28 段）

paragraphs.en: `So you did, old fellow!' said the others.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 29 段）

paragraphs.en: `We must burn the house down!' said the Rabbit's voice; and Alice called out as loud as she could, `If you do. I'll set Dinah at you!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 30 段）

paragraphs.en: There was a dead silence instantly, and Alice thought to herself, `I wonder what they WILL do next! If they had any sense, they'd take the roof off.' After a minute or two, they began moving about again, and Alice heard the Rabbit say, `A barrowful will do, to begin with.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 31 段）

paragraphs.en: `A barrowful of WHAT?' thought Alice; but she had not long to doubt, for the next moment a shower of little pebbles came rattling in at the window, and some of them hit her in the face. `I'll put a stop to this,' she said to herself, and shouted out, `You'd better not do that again!' which produced another dead silence.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 32 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice noticed with some surprise that the pebbles were all turning into little cakes as they lay on the floor, and a bright idea came into her head. `If I eat one of these cakes,' she thought, `it's sure to make SOME change in my size; and as it can't possibly make me larger, it must make me smaller, I suppose.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 33 段）

paragraphs.en: So she swallowed one of the cakes, and was delighted to find that she began shrinking directly. As soon as she was small enough to get through the door, she ran out of the house, and found quite a crowd of little animals and birds waiting outside. The poor little Lizard, Bill, was in the middle, being held up by two guinea-pigs, who were giving it something out of a bottle. They all made a rush at Alice the moment she appeared; but she ran off as hard as she could, and soon found herself safe in a thick wood.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 34 段）

paragraphs.en: `The first thing I've got to do,' said Alice to herself, as she wandered about in the wood, `is to grow to my right size again; and the second thing is to find my way into that lovely garden. I think that will be the best plan.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 35 段）

paragraphs.en: It sounded an excellent plan, no doubt, and very neatly and simply arranged; the only difficulty was, that she had not the smallest idea how to set about it; and while she was peering about anxiously among the trees, a little sharp bark just over her head made her look up in a great hurry.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 36 段）

paragraphs.en: An enormous puppy was looking down at her with large round eyes, and feebly stretching out one paw, trying to touch her. `Poor little thing!' said Alice, in a coaxing tone, and she tried hard to whistle to it; but she was terribly frightened all the time at the thought that it might be hungry, in which case it would be very likely to eat her up in spite of all her coaxing.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 37 段）

paragraphs.en: Hardly knowing what she did, she picked up a little bit of stick, and held it out to the puppy; whereupon the puppy jumped into the air off all its feet at once, with a yelp of delight, and rushed at the stick, and made believe to worry it; then Alice dodged behind a great thistle, to keep herself from being run over; and the moment she appeared on the other side, the puppy made another rush at the stick, and tumbled head over heels in its hurry to get hold of it; then Alice, thinking it was very like having a game of play with a cart-horse, and expecting every moment to be trampled under its feet, ran round the thistle again; then the puppy began a series of short charges at the stick, running a very little way forwards each time and a long way back, and barking hoarsely all the while, till at last it sat down a good way off, panting, with its tongue hanging out of its mouth, and its great eyes half shut.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 38 段）

paragraphs.en: This seemed to Alice a good opportunity for making her escape; so she set off at once, and ran till she was quite tired and out of breath, and till the puppy's bark sounded quite faint in the distance.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 39 段）

paragraphs.en: `And yet what a dear little puppy it was!' said Alice, as she leant against a buttercup to rest herself, and fanned herself with one of the leaves: `I should have liked teaching it tricks very much, if--if I'd only been the right size to do it! Oh dear! I'd nearly forgotten that I've got to grow up again! Let me see--how IS it to be managed? I suppose I ought to eat or drink something or other; but the great question is, what?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 40 段）

paragraphs.en: The great question certainly was, what? Alice looked all round her at the flowers and the blades of grass, but she did not see anything that looked like the right thing to eat or drink under the circumstances. There was a large mushroom growing near her, about the same height as herself; and when she had looked under it, and on both sides of it, and behind it, it occurred to her that she might as well look and see what was on the top of it.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 41 段）

paragraphs.en: She stretched herself up on tiptoe, and peeped over the edge of the mushroom, and her eyes immediately met those of a large caterpillar, that was sitting on the top with its arms folded, quietly smoking a long hookah, and taking not the smallest notice of her or of anything else.
paragraphs.zh: （第 4 章 · 白兔差遣小比尔 第 42 段）

paragraphs.en:
CHAPTER V
Advice from a Caterpillar
paragraphs.zh: 第五章 · 毛毛虫的建议
paragraphs.chapterTitleZh: 第五章 · 毛毛虫的建议

paragraphs.en: The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 1 段）

paragraphs.en: `Who are YOU?' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 2 段）

paragraphs.en: This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied, rather shyly, `I--I hardly know, sir, just at present-- at least I know who I WAS when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been changed several times since then.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 3 段）

paragraphs.en: `What do you mean by that?' said the Caterpillar sternly. `Explain yourself!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 4 段）

paragraphs.en: `I can't explain MYSELF, I'm afraid, sir' said Alice, `because I'm not myself, you see.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 5 段）

paragraphs.en: `I don't see,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 6 段）

paragraphs.en: `I'm afraid I can't put it more clearly,' Alice replied very politely, `for I can't understand it myself to begin with; and being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 7 段）

paragraphs.en: `It isn't,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 8 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, perhaps you haven't found it so yet,' said Alice; `but when you have to turn into a chrysalis--you will some day, you know--and then after that into a butterfly, I should think you'll feel it a little queer, won't you?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 9 段）

paragraphs.en: `Not a bit,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 10 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, perhaps your feelings may be different,' said Alice; `all I know is, it would feel very queer to ME.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 11 段）

paragraphs.en: `You!' said the Caterpillar contemptuously. `Who are YOU?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 12 段）

paragraphs.en: Which brought them back again to the beginning of the conversation. Alice felt a little irritated at the Caterpillar's making such VERY short remarks, and she drew herself up and said, very gravely, `I think, you ought to tell me who YOU are, first.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 13 段）

paragraphs.en: `Why?' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 14 段）

paragraphs.en: Here was another puzzling question; and as Alice could not think of any good reason, and as the Caterpillar seemed to be in a VERY unpleasant state of mind, she turned away.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 15 段）

paragraphs.en: `Come back!' the Caterpillar called after her. `I've something important to say!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 16 段）

paragraphs.en: This sounded promising, certainly: Alice turned and came back again.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 17 段）

paragraphs.en: `Keep your temper,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 18 段）

paragraphs.en: `Is that all?' said Alice, swallowing down her anger as well as she could.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 19 段）

paragraphs.en: `No,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 20 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice thought she might as well wait, as she had nothing else to do, and perhaps after all it might tell her something worth hearing. For some minutes it puffed away without speaking, but at last it unfolded its arms, took the hookah out of its mouth again, and said, `So you think you're changed, do you?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 21 段）

paragraphs.en: `I'm afraid I am, sir,' said Alice; `I can't remember things as I used--and I don't keep the same size for ten minutes together!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 22 段）

paragraphs.en: `Can't remember WHAT things?' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 23 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, I've tried to say "HOW DOTH THE LITTLE BUSY BEE," but it all came different!' Alice replied in a very melancholy voice.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 24 段）

paragraphs.en: `Repeat, "YOU ARE OLD, FATHER WILLIAM,"' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 25 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice folded her hands, and began:--
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 26 段）

paragraphs.en: `You are old, Father William,' the young man said, `And your hair has become very white; And yet you incessantly stand on your head-- Do you think, at your age, it is right?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 27 段）

paragraphs.en: `In my youth,' Father William replied to his son, `I feared it might injure the brain; But, now that I'm perfectly sure I have none, Why, I do it again and again.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 28 段）

paragraphs.en: `You are old,' said the youth, `as I mentioned before, And have grown most uncommonly fat; Yet you turned a back-somersault in at the door-- Pray, what is the reason of that?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 29 段）

paragraphs.en: `In my youth,' said the sage, as he shook his grey locks, `I kept all my limbs very supple By the use of this ointment--one shilling the box-- Allow me to sell you a couple?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 30 段）

paragraphs.en: `You are old,' said the youth, `and your jaws are too weak For anything tougher than suet; Yet you finished the goose, with the bones and the beak-- Pray how did you manage to do it?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 31 段）

paragraphs.en: `In my youth,' said his father, `I took to the law, And argued each case with my wife; And the muscular strength, which it gave to my jaw, Has lasted the rest of my life.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 32 段）

paragraphs.en: `You are old,' said the youth, `one would hardly suppose That your eye was as steady as ever; Yet you balanced an eel on the end of your nose-- What made you so awfully clever?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 33 段）

paragraphs.en: `I have answered three questions, and that is enough,' Said his father; `don't give yourself airs! Do you think I can listen all day to such stuff? Be off, or I'll kick you down stairs!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 34 段）

paragraphs.en: `That is not said right,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 35 段）

paragraphs.en: `Not QUITE right, I'm afraid,' said Alice, timidly; `some of the words have got altered.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 36 段）

paragraphs.en: `It is wrong from beginning to end,' said the Caterpillar decidedly, and there was silence for some minutes.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 37 段）

paragraphs.en: The Caterpillar was the first to speak.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 38 段）

paragraphs.en: `What size do you want to be?' it asked.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 39 段）

paragraphs.en: `Oh, I'm not particular as to size,' Alice hastily replied; `only one doesn't like changing so often, you know.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 40 段）

paragraphs.en: `I DON'T know,' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 41 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice said nothing: she had never been so much contradicted in her life before, and she felt that she was losing her temper.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 42 段）

paragraphs.en: `Are you content now?' said the Caterpillar.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 43 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, I should like to be a LITTLE larger, sir, if you wouldn't mind,' said Alice: `three inches is such a wretched height to be.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 44 段）

paragraphs.en: `It is a very good height indeed!' said the Caterpillar angrily, rearing itself upright as it spoke (it was exactly three inches high).
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 45 段）

paragraphs.en: `But I'm not used to it!' pleaded poor Alice in a piteous tone. And she thought of herself, `I wish the creatures wouldn't be so easily offended!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 46 段）

paragraphs.en: `You'll get used to it in time,' said the Caterpillar; and it put the hookah into its mouth and began smoking again.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 47 段）

paragraphs.en: This time Alice waited patiently until it chose to speak again. In a minute or two the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth and yawned once or twice, and shook itself. Then it got down off the mushroom, and crawled away in the grass, merely remarking as it went, `One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 48 段）

paragraphs.en: `One side of WHAT? The other side of WHAT?' thought Alice to herself.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 49 段）

paragraphs.en: `Of the mushroom,' said the Caterpillar, just as if she had asked it aloud; and in another moment it was out of sight.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 50 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice remained looking thoughtfully at the mushroom for a minute, trying to make out which were the two sides of it; and as it was perfectly round, she found this a very difficult question. However, at last she stretched her arms round it as far as they would go, and broke off a bit of the edge with each hand.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 51 段）

paragraphs.en: `And now which is which?' she said to herself, and nibbled a little of the right-hand bit to try the effect: the next moment she felt a violent blow underneath her chin: it had struck her foot!
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 52 段）

paragraphs.en: She was a good deal frightened by this very sudden change, but she felt that there was no time to be lost, as she was shrinking rapidly; so she set to work at once to eat some of the other bit. Her chin was pressed so closely against her foot, that there was hardly room to open her mouth; but she did it at last, and managed to swallow a morsel of the lefthand bit.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 53 段）

paragraphs.en: `Come, my head's free at last!' said Alice in a tone of delight, which changed into alarm in another moment, when she found that her shoulders were nowhere to be found: all she could see, when she looked down, was an immense length of neck, which seemed to rise like a stalk out of a sea of green leaves that lay far below her.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 54 段）

paragraphs.en: `What CAN all that green stuff be?' said Alice. `And where HAVE my shoulders got to? And oh, my poor hands, how is it I can't see you?' She was moving them about as she spoke, but no result seemed to follow, except a little shaking among the distant green leaves.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 55 段）

paragraphs.en: As there seemed to be no chance of getting her hands up to her head, she tried to get her head down to them, and was delighted to find that her neck would bend about easily in any direction, like a serpent. She had just succeeded in curving it down into a graceful zigzag, and was going to dive in among the leaves, which she found to be nothing but the tops of the trees under which she had been wandering, when a sharp hiss made her draw back in a hurry: a large pigeon had flown into her face, and was beating her violently with its wings.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 56 段）

paragraphs.en: `Serpent!' screamed the Pigeon.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 57 段）

paragraphs.en: `I'm NOT a serpent!' said Alice indignantly. `Let me alone!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 58 段）

paragraphs.en: `Serpent, I say again!' repeated the Pigeon, but in a more subdued tone, and added with a kind of sob, `I've tried every way, and nothing seems to suit them!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 59 段）

paragraphs.en: `I haven't the least idea what you're talking about,' said Alice.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 60 段）

paragraphs.en: `I've tried the roots of trees, and I've tried banks, and I've tried hedges,' the Pigeon went on, without attending to her; `but those serpents! There's no pleasing them!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 61 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice was more and more puzzled, but she thought there was no use in saying anything more till the Pigeon had finished.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 62 段）

paragraphs.en: `As if it wasn't trouble enough hatching the eggs,' said the Pigeon; `but I must be on the look-out for serpents night and day! Why, I haven't had a wink of sleep these three weeks!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 63 段）

paragraphs.en: `I'm very sorry you've been annoyed,' said Alice, who was beginning to see its meaning.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 64 段）

paragraphs.en: `And just as I'd taken the highest tree in the wood,' continued the Pigeon, raising its voice to a shriek, `and just as I was thinking I should be free of them at last, they must needs come wriggling down from the sky! Ugh, Serpent!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 65 段）

paragraphs.en: `But I'm NOT a serpent, I tell you!' said Alice. `I'm a--I'm a--'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 66 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well! WHAT are you?' said the Pigeon. `I can see you're trying to invent something!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 67 段）

paragraphs.en: `I--I'm a little girl,' said Alice, rather doubtfully, as she remembered the number of changes she had gone through that day.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 68 段）

paragraphs.en: `A likely story indeed!' said the Pigeon in a tone of the deepest contempt. `I've seen a good many little girls in my time, but never ONE with such a neck as that! No, no! You're a serpent; and there's no use denying it. I suppose you'll be telling me next that you never tasted an egg!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 69 段）

paragraphs.en: `I HAVE tasted eggs, certainly,' said Alice, who was a very truthful child; `but little girls eat eggs quite as much as serpents do, you know.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 70 段）

paragraphs.en: `I don't believe it,' said the Pigeon; `but if they do, why then they're a kind of serpent, that's all I can say.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 71 段）

paragraphs.en: This was such a new idea to Alice, that she was quite silent for a minute or two, which gave the Pigeon the opportunity of adding, `You're looking for eggs, I know THAT well enough; and what does it matter to me whether you're a little girl or a serpent?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 72 段）

paragraphs.en: `It matters a good deal to ME,' said Alice hastily; `but I'm not looking for eggs, as it happens; and if I was, I shouldn't want YOURS: I don't like them raw.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 73 段）

paragraphs.en: `Well, be off, then!' said the Pigeon in a sulky tone, as it settled down again into its nest. Alice crouched down among the trees as well as she could, for her neck kept getting entangled among the branches, and every now and then she had to stop and untwist it. After a while she remembered that she still held the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, and growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 74 段）

paragraphs.en: It was so long since she had been anything near the right size, that it felt quite strange at first; but she got used to it in a few minutes, and began talking to herself, as usual. `Come, there's half my plan done now! How puzzling all these changes are! I'm never sure what I'm going to be, from one minute to another! However, I've got back to my right size: the next thing is, to get into that beautiful garden--how IS that to be done, I wonder?' As she said this, she came suddenly upon an open place, with a little house in it about four feet high. `Whoever lives there,' thought Alice, `it'll never do to come upon them THIS size: why, I should frighten them out of their wits!' So she began nibbling at the righthand bit again, and did not venture to go near the house till she had brought herself down to nine inches high.
paragraphs.zh: （第 5 章 · 毛毛虫的建议 第 75 段）

paragraphs.en:
CHAPTER VI
Pig and Pepper
paragraphs.zh: 第六章 · 小猪与胡椒
paragraphs.chapterTitleZh: 第六章 · 小猪与胡椒

paragraphs.en: For a minute or two she stood looking at the house, and wondering what to do next, when suddenly a footman in livery came running out of the wood--(she considered him to be a footman because he was in livery: otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish)--and rapped loudly at the door with his knuckles. It was opened by another footman in livery, with a round face, and large eyes like a frog; and both footmen, Alice noticed, had powdered hair that curled all over their heads. She felt very curious to know what it was all about, and crept a little way out of the wood to listen.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 1 段）

paragraphs.en: The Fish-Footman began by producing from under his arm a great letter, nearly as large as himself, and this he handed over to the other, saying, in a solemn tone, `For the Duchess. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet.' The Frog-Footman repeated, in the same solemn tone, only changing the order of the words a little, `From the Queen. An invitation for the Duchess to play croquet.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 2 段）

paragraphs.en: Then they both bowed low, and their curls got entangled together.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 3 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice laughed so much at this, that she had to run back into the wood for fear of their hearing her; and when she next peeped out the Fish-Footman was gone, and the other was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up into the sky.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 4 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice went timidly up to the door, and knocked.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 5 段）

paragraphs.en: `There's no sort of use in knocking,' said the Footman, `and that for two reasons. First, because I'm on the same side of the door as you are; secondly, because they're making such a noise inside, no one could possibly hear you.' And certainly there was a most extraordinary noise going on within--a constant howling and sneezing, and every now and then a great crash, as if a dish or kettle had been broken to pieces.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 6 段）

paragraphs.en: `Please, then,' said Alice, `how am I to get in?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 7 段）

paragraphs.en: `There might be some sense in your knocking,' the Footman went on without attending to her, `if we had the door between us. For instance, if you were INSIDE, you might knock, and I could let you out, you know.' He was looking up into the sky all the time he was speaking, and this Alice thought decidedly uncivil. `But perhaps he can't help it,' she said to herself; `his eyes are so VERY nearly at the top of his head. But at any rate he might answer questions.--How am I to get in?' she repeated, aloud.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 8 段）

paragraphs.en: `I shall sit here,' the Footman remarked, `till tomorrow--'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 9 段）

paragraphs.en: At this moment the door of the house opened, and a large plate came skimming out, straight at the Footman's head: it just grazed his nose, and broke to pieces against one of the trees behind him.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 10 段）

paragraphs.en: `--or next day, maybe,' the Footman continued in the same tone, exactly as if nothing had happened.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 11 段）

paragraphs.en: `How am I to get in?' asked Alice again, in a louder tone.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 12 段）

paragraphs.en: `ARE you to get in at all?' said the Footman. `That's the first question, you know.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 13 段）

paragraphs.en: It was, no doubt: only Alice did not like to be told so. `It's really dreadful,' she muttered to herself, `the way all the creatures argue. It's enough to drive one crazy!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 14 段）

paragraphs.en: The Footman seemed to think this a good opportunity for repeating his remark, with variations. `I shall sit here,' he said, `on and off, for days and days.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 15 段）

paragraphs.en: `But what am I to do?' said Alice.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 16 段）

paragraphs.en: `Anything you like,' said the Footman, and began whistling.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 17 段）

paragraphs.en: `Oh, there's no use in talking to him,' said Alice desperately: `he's perfectly idiotic!' And she opened the door and went in.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 18 段）

paragraphs.en: The door led right into a large kitchen, which was full of smoke from one end to the other: the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby; the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron which seemed to be full of soup.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 19 段）

paragraphs.en: `There's certainly too much pepper in that soup!' Alice said to herself, as well as she could for sneezing.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 20 段）

paragraphs.en: There was certainly too much of it in the air. Even the Duchess sneezed occasionally; and as for the baby, it was sneezing and howling alternately without a moment's pause. The only things in the kitchen that did not sneeze, were the cook, and a large cat which was sitting on the hearth and grinning from ear to ear.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 21 段）

paragraphs.en: `Please would you tell me,' said Alice, a little timidly, for she was not quite sure whether it was good manners for her to speak first, `why your cat grins like that?'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 22 段）

paragraphs.en: `It's a Cheshire cat,' said the Duchess, `and that's why. Pig!'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 23 段）

paragraphs.en: She said the last word with such sudden violence that Alice quite jumped; but she saw in another moment that it was addressed to the baby, and not to her, so she took courage, and went on again:--
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 24 段）

paragraphs.en: `I didn't know that Cheshire cats always grinned; in fact, I didn't know that cats COULD grin.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 25 段）

paragraphs.en: `They all can,' said the Duchess; `and most of 'em do.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 26 段）

paragraphs.en: `I don't know of any that do,' Alice said very politely, feeling quite pleased to have got into a conversation.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 27 段）

paragraphs.en: `You don't know much,' said the Duchess; `and that's a fact.'
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 28 段）

paragraphs.en: Alice did not at all like the tone of this remark, and thought it would be as well to introduce some other subject of conversation. While she was trying to fix on one, the cook took the cauldron of soup off the fire, and at once set to work throwing everything within her reach at the Duchess and the baby --the fire-irons came first; then followed a shower of saucepans, plates, and dishes. The Duchess took no notice of them even when they hit her; and the baby was howling so much already, that it was quite impossible to say whether the blows hurt it or not.
paragraphs.zh: （第 6 章 · 小猪与胡椒 第 29 段）

paragraphs.en: `Oh, PLEASE mind what you're doing!' cried Alice, jumping up and down in an agony of terror. `Oh, there goes his PRECIOUS nose'; as an unusually large saucepan flew close by it, and very nearly carried it off.
